notes.meaning: King Xerxes promoted Haman to the highest office in the Persian empire, placing him above all the other nobles. Haman is called an Agagite, linking him to the ancient royal family of the Amalekites, who were long-standing enemies of Israel. Even in royal courts where evil leaders rise to high places, God remains in control of history.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that 'Agagite' refers to a Persian province or home district rather than descent from King Agag of Amalek.

notes.meaning: The king commanded all palace officials at the gate to bow down to the ground and honor Haman. Mordecai refused to kneel or prostrate himself before him. This Persian homage often treated the leader as a god, which violated the Jewish law against giving divine worship to any human.

The other royal officials noticed Mordecai standing upright and asked why he was breaking the king's direct order. They warned him that disobeying a royal command put his life in serious danger. Standing firm for God often invites questions and pressure from the people around us.

The palace servants urged Mordecai every day to comply, but he would not change his mind. Mordecai explained that he was a Jew, which meant his religious convictions forbade such worship. The servants then reported this to Haman to see whether Mordecai's religious reason would be allowed.

Once Haman noticed that Mordecai refused to bow, he burned with intense anger. His immense pride could not tolerate even one person withholding homage from him. Unchecked pride easily turns into dangerous rage when our self-importance is challenged.

Haman felt that executing only Mordecai was too small a revenge for his wounded pride. When he learned Mordecai was a Jew, he decided to wipe out every Jewish person in the entire Persian empire. His personal grudge quickly grew into a desire for total genocide.

In the first month of the year, Haman and his astrologers cast lots, called Pur, to pick the most lucky day to carry out the massacre. The lot fell on the twelfth month, nearly a full year away. God used Haman's own superstitions to provide plenty of time for His people to be saved.

differ.view: Some Baptists point out that casting lots to tell the future is forbidden occult practice in Scripture, highlighting Haman's pagan defiance of God.

notes.meaning: Haman told King Xerxes that a certain unnamed group was scattered across all the provinces, living by their own customs and ignoring royal laws. He claimed it was dangerous and unprofitable for the king to let them remain. Haman used clever half-truths to make a peaceful, law-abiding minority sound like dangerous rebels.

Haman asked the king to issue a written decree to destroy this entire people. To make up for any loss in tax revenue, Haman offered to pay ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasury. He was willing to spend an enormous personal fortune just to satisfy his hatred.

King Xerxes took off his royal signet ring and handed it to Haman, the enemy of the Jews. Stamping a document with this ring gave an order the full, unchangeable power of royal law. The king carelessly handed over absolute authority without even asking who the condemned people were.

The king told Haman to keep his money and do whatever he wanted with the people. Xerxes treated the lives of thousands of his subjects as if they were completely worthless. Uncaring rulers often cause immense suffering when they act with blind indifference.

On the thirteenth day of the first month, the royal scribes were called to write out Haman's decree. The order was translated into the script and language of every province and ethnic group across the empire. It was published in the king's name and sealed with the royal signet ring so it could not be repealed.

Messengers carried the letters to every royal province with orders to slaughter all Jews—men, women, and children—on a single day, the thirteenth day of Adar. The decree also allowed the killers to seize all their property and goods. Haman used greed to tempt the public into joining the violent attack.

A copy of the decree was published openly in every province so that all the citizens would be ready for that day. It turned neighbors against neighbors by giving legal permission for murder. Even when state laws are profoundly wicked, God's people can trust His higher authority.

The couriers rushed out by the king's command, and the decree was published in the capital city of Susa. While the king and Haman sat down to drink, the ordinary citizens of the city were thrown into confusion and alarm. The contrast shows the cold cruelty of the leaders against the shock of everyday people.
